Processing a Real GC-MS/FID Sample

The problem

A fuel or process sample leaves the instrument as three separate things: an FID peak table (quantitative, but anonymous), an MSD peak table (identified, but on a slightly different time axis), and a library-search export that names the MSD peaks. A client wants one table of compounds with amounts, plus a summary of chemical families and elements.

fidms replaces the old “Automated Polyarc” Excel/VBA macro for this job. This vignette follows one real sample, D319, end to end, first in code and then through the local Shiny app. Along the way it points out each place where the analyst has to supply something the instrument files cannot know.

What goes in

The three exports fidms reads are bundled with this vignette as CSV files, copied from the Agilent D319.D data directory. The raw data.ms scan file in that directory enables the optional hydrocarbon-class analysis; it is not bundled, so that section only runs where the .D directory is available.

fid_csv    <- "FIDpeaks.csv"
msd_csv    <- "MSDpeaks.csv"
search_csv <- "MSDsearch.csv"

file.exists(c(fid_csv, msd_csv, search_csv))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE

Only the three CSVs are required; the raw scans are additive.

Sample properties only the analyst knows

Several numbers feed directly into the reported weight percents, and none of them are in the instrument files:

Property Why it is needed
Sample number, name, project code, analyst(s) Report headers and output file name
Density (g/mL) Converts \(\mu\)g/mL to weight percent
Methanol and water (wt. %) Measured separately (e.g. Karl Fischer); reported alongside the GC result so totals can approach 100
Dilution factor Corrects amounts for any dilution before injection 
info <- fidms:::.sample_info(
  sample_id       = "D319",
  sample_name     = "Demo fuel sample",
  project_code    = "DEMO",
  analyst         = "PB",
  density         = 0.8519,
  methanol_wt_pct = 0,
  water_wt_pct    = 53 / 1e4, # 53 ppm = 0.0053 wt. %
  dilution        = 1
)
info$analyst
#> [1] "PB"

The metadata constructor is internal, because the Shiny app is its main caller; in code you build it directly. Multiple analysts are joined with a slash. The density and water content are the measured values for this sample; water is entered in weight percent, so 53 ppm becomes 0.0053.

Processing in code

Alignment and identification

prepare_peaks() is the first half of the pipeline. It parses the files, finds the time offset between the FID and MSD detectors, matches peaks across them, attaches library identities, merges split peaks and fills in formulae for unidentified peaks by interpolation.

prep <- prepare_peaks(fid_csv, msd_csv, search_csv)
c(peaks = nrow(prep$peaks), shift_min = prep$shift)
#>     peaks shift_min 
#>   650.000     0.009
table(prep$peaks$origin)
#> 
#> extrapolated interpolated          msd 
#>           90          247          313

The search found an MS-to-FID offset of 0.009 minutes, which is small. Most peaks align to an MSD peak; the few interpolated and extrapolated ones have no library identity, so their formulae are estimated from neighbours. Those are the rows to treat with the most caution in a client report.

Optional: hydrocarbon classes from raw scans

When the raw data.ms is available, the ASTM D2425 class-ion deconvolution can assign hydrocarbon classes to peaks the library could not name, instead of leaving them to interpolation. These helpers are internal; the Shiny app calls them for you whenever you give it a .D directory.

scan_matrix  <- fidms:::.read_ms_scan_matrix(d_dir)
class_traces <- fidms:::.build_class_ion_traces(scan_matrix)

prep_cls <- prepare_peaks(
  fid_csv, msd_csv, search_csv,
  class_traces = class_traces,
  scan_matrix  = scan_matrix
)
table(prep_cls$peaks$assignment_tier, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>   A   B   C   D   M 
#> 237  71 256   9  77

The assignment tiers record how much evidence supports each peak (library hit, class-ion solve, mixed region, or none). Reading the raw scan file takes several seconds, which is why this step is opt-in.

Quantitation

Calibration is the second half. The default style = "slope" uses the packaged calibration table for compounds with targets and a Polyarc relative response for everything else. Dilution and density come from the sample metadata.

peaks <- calibrate(
  prep_cls$peaks,
  style    = "slope",
  dilution = info$dilution,
  density  = info$density
)
res <- summarize_report(peaks, info, shift = prep_cls$shift)
res$totals[c("gc_recovery", "total")]
#> $gc_recovery
#> [1] 88.90453
#> 
#> $total
#> [1] 88.90983

GC recovery is the sum of the quantified, non-solvent compounds in weight percent. A value well below 100 after adding methanol and water would suggest undetected material, so the number is worth comparing with expectations for the sample type rather than accepting automatically.

Internal-standard quantitation

If the sample contains a compound that can serve as an internal reference, style = "internal" normalises the sample to 100% against it. Choosing that peak is a judgement call, so fidms proposes one and checks its quality.

ref <- fidms:::.suggest_reference_peak(prep_cls$peaks)
ref[c("peak_index", "name", "area_percent", "score", "approved")]
#> $peak_index
#> [1] 495
#> 
#> $name
#> [1] "9-Octadecenoic acid, methyl ester, (E)-"
#> 
#> $area_percent
#> [1] 3.881259
#> 
#> $score
#> [1] 97.56
#> 
#> $approved
#> [1] TRUE

Here the suggestion is the largest peak that passes the quality check (a good library match and a reasonable share of the total area). approved is TRUE when the largest peak itself qualified; otherwise the next best qualifying peak is offered. The analyst may override it by choosing any other peak index.

peaks_is <- calibrate(
  prep_cls$peaks,
  style          = "internal",
  reference_peak = ref$peak_index,
  dilution       = info$dilution,
  density        = info$density
)
res_is <- summarize_report(peaks_is, info, shift = prep_cls$shift)
round(res_is$totals$gc_recovery, 1)
#> [1] 88

The internal-standard recovery differs from the slope-style result, because amounts are now scaled relative to the reference peak rather than from the calibration curves. Here the reference is a library-identified methyl ester making up a few percent of the total area, so the result depends on how well that one peak represents the sample. Comparing the two recoveries is a useful sanity check on the choice of reference.

Reading the summary

fam <- res$families
fam <- fam[fam$wt_pct > 0, ]
op <- par(mar = c(4, 9, 1, 1))
barplot(rev(fam$wt_pct), names.arg = rev(fam$compound_type), horiz = TRUE,
        las = 1, xlab = "wt. %")

par(op)

The sample is dominated by aromatics and the hydrocarbon families, with a smaller oxygenate fraction. Families are assigned programmatically from formulae and names, so the compound types are indicative and, as the report notes state, not a substitute for a standard PIONA analysis.

The per-compound table that the client sees is built by total_compound_table():

tc <- total_compound_table(res, include_class_ion = TRUE)
head(tc[, c("Peak No.", "Compound Name", "Retention Time",
            "Area (FID)", "Amount (ug/mL)")], 8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   `Peak No.` `Compound Name`      `Retention Time` `Area (FID)` `Amount (ug/mL)`
#>   <chr>      <chr>                <chr>                   <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 1          Cyclopropene         1.327                   3898.             5.82
#> 2 2          Unknown, Interpolat… 1.377                  11609.            17.9 
#> 3 3          Butane               1.404                  71176.           116.  
#> 4 4          Butane, 2-methyl-    1.496                 122781.           198.  
#> 5 5          Pentane              1.544                 206784.           334.  
#> 6 6          <NA>                 1.596                   7822.            NA   
#> 7 7          Methylene chloride   1.645               27526903.        261396.  
#> 8 8          Pentane, 2-methyl-   1.757                 674695.          1084.

Unmatched peaks have no compound name, and combined peaks print the sentinel "Combined FID Peaks" instead of a retention time, which is why that column is character.

Writing the reports

Both writers take the summarised result. The Excel report has a Total Compound sheet and a Summary sheet.

xlsx <- write_excel_report(res, file.path(tempdir(), "DEMO_D319_GC-MS-FID.xlsx"))
openxlsx::getSheetNames(xlsx)
#> [1] "D319 Total Compound Report" "D319 Summary Report"

The PDF report is rendered from a Quarto template, so it needs Quarto and a LaTeX engine installed. The chunk below is not evaluated when the vignette is built; the image after it is the first page of the report produced from this sample.

write_pdf_report(res, "DEMO_D319_GC-MS-FID.pdf")
First page of the generated PDF: sample header and QC counts, followed by the Total Compound table.

The header block repeats the sample metadata and the headline numbers (GC recovery, peak counts, MS/FID offset), so a reader can check the report against the inputs without opening anything else. Compounds without a library identity show as NA. The remaining pages continue the compound table and end with the Summary Report.

The same workflow in the Shiny app

Everything above is available through a local Shiny app. It runs on your machine and is not meant for deployment, so client data stays local.

fidms::run_app()

The app needs shiny, bslib and DT. The screenshots below were captured from a real run on D319.D.

1. Point the app at the data

The app on start-up: the Files panel accepts a .D directory and/or uploads of the three CSVs.

Enter the .D directory and the app uses the CSVs found inside it, and also reads data.ms for the hydrocarbon-class analysis. Uploaded CSVs take precedence over files in the directory.

2. Enter the sample properties

The Sample panel holds the metadata the instrument files do not contain.

This is the same information as the metadata object in code. The sample number is required; processing does not start without it.

3. Choose processing options

The Processing panel: alignment engine, calibration style and shift-search parameters.

The defaults reproduce the macro’s behaviour. The alignment engine (grid or gcalignr) and the shift parameters correspond to fidms_params(). The two engines are not expected to agree exactly, and the production default is still an open question. Choosing Internal standard adds a panel showing the suggested reference peak, which you can override by selecting a row in the Peaks tab.

4. Process and review the peaks

The Peaks tab after pressing Process sample.

Pressing Process sample runs the same steps as the code above. The Peaks table is the Total Compound table; with a .D directory it also carries the class-ion columns to the right.

5. Check the summary

The Summary tab: compound types, elements and QC counts.

These are the numbers that go on the Summary Report. They match the code-based result because both paths call the same functions.

6. Retention-index anchors and class features

The RI points tab is editable; the polynomial is refit from whatever is there.

The retention-index model is refit at run time from these anchors, so editing a point changes how library hits are cross-checked.

The MS Class Features tab lists class sub-features detected inside each FID peak.

This audit table is only populated when raw scan data was supplied.

7. Download the reports

The Excel report and PDF report buttons call write_excel_report() and write_pdf_report() on the current result, named {project code}_{sample number}_GC-MS-FID.

Summary

The workflow is prepare_peaks(), then calibrate(), then summarize_report(), then a report writer; the app wraps the same sequence. The inputs to supply yourself are the sample metadata (density, methanol, water, dilution), the calibration style, and, for internal standardisation, the reference peak. Worth checking by eye: interpolated peaks, GC recovery, and the choice of alignment engine.

Screenshots are generated by data-raw/capture_app_screenshots.R; rerun it after any UI change.
